title: Math for my first grader
short: The workbook I landed on when the school did not send one home this year.

images.alt: Spectrum Math Grade 1 workbook open on a kitchen table with a pencil

quickTake: Looks and works like the workbook schools send home: clear pages, one skill at a time, answer key in the back.
Covers the real first-grade list: addition and subtraction within 100, place value, fact families, shapes, measurement, time.
Ten to twenty minutes a page. A first grader can do most of it without you hovering.

p: Last year the school sent a kindergarten math workbook home and it quietly did the job. A page a night, no drama. This year nothing came home, so I went looking for the closest thing to that book.

I compared the ones parents and teachers keep recommending: Spectrum, Brain Quest, School Zone Big Math, Math Mammoth, and Math with Confidence. Spectrum is the one that matches what a first-grade classroom actually teaches, in the order the teacher is likely teaching it.

body.h: How it compares to the others
p: Brain Quest is the fun one. Stickers, a progress map, activities instead of rows of problems. If your kid groans at worksheets, start there.
School Zone Big Math 1-2 is the value pick. Over 300 pages, and it stretches into second grade, so it lasts.

Math Mammoth and Math with Confidence are the ones homeschool parents swear by, and they are excellent. They also ask more of you as the teacher. For plain daily practice that mirrors school, Spectrum wins.

body.h: What to know before you buy
p: It is standards-aligned, so the topics should line up with what the teacher is doing. Still, open the Look Inside preview on Amazon and match it to where your kid is right now. The pretest at the start of each chapter helps with that.
Pages do not tear out cleanly. If you want loose sheets for the fridge, cut them or copy them.
It is not flashy. That is the point. If you need flashy, see Brain Quest above.
Parents of a first grader who want a page a night without hunting for printables. Teachers who want a reliable extra-practice book. Anyone whose school stopped sending one home.

verdict.buy: You want the closest thing to a school-sent math workbook for a first grader, with an answer key and no setup.
verdict.skip: Your kid needs to be won over first. Get Brain Quest Math 1st Grade, then come back to this one.

title: The book I hand to anyone who says they are bad at learning
short: Three habits that actually make practice stick, explained for adults.

images.alt: Make It Stick open on a desk next to a notebook

quickTake: Explains why re-reading feels productive and does almost nothing.
Gives you three habits that actually move the needle: retrieval, spacing, interleaving.
Readable in a weekend. You will want to argue with it, then try it.

p: I teach music. Every year a student tells me they practiced for an hour and it still did not stick. I used to think that was a motivation problem. This book is where I learned it was a method problem.

I changed how I run the first ten minutes of class. Instead of reviewing, I quiz. Instead of drilling one thing, I mix three. Within a month the same kids were retaining more with less time. Same kids, same me, different method.
I have since bought copies for two colleagues and one parent who asked how I got her kid to practice without a fight.

body.h: What to know before you buy
p: It is written for adults, not students. If you want to hand it to a teenager, read it first and translate the ideas.
The middle chapters repeat themselves a little. Skim where you need to. The ideas hold up.
Teachers, parents, and anyone learning something hard as an adult: an instrument, a language, a certification. If you only read one book about how learning works, make it this one.

verdict.buy: You teach, you parent, or you are learning something hard and tired of forgetting it.
verdict.skip: You want a workbook with exercises. This is the why, not the drills.

product: Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning

title: A sustain pedal for my keyboard lab
short: The pedal I put on every keyboard after the cheap ones kept sliding away.

images.alt: Sustain pedal on a classroom floor under a keyboard stand
Close-up of the pedal's rubber base
Row of keyboards in a music classroom

quickTake: Heavy enough that it does not creep across tile floors mid-song.
Feels like a real piano pedal, which matters when students move to an acoustic.
Has a polarity switch, so it works with keyboards that invert the signal.

p: The pedals that come free with keyboards are plastic squares that slide. Beginners end up chasing them with their foot instead of playing. I needed something with weight and a rubber base for a room full of them.
Bought one to test, then outfitted the lab. Two years in, zero failures. Kids stopped asking me to fix their pedal mid-class, which is the whole point.
The polarity switch saved me once when a donated keyboard sustained everything until I flipped it.

body.h: What to know before you buy
p: The cable is not detachable. If a student yanks it, you replace the pedal, not the cable. Tape the cable down if the room is chaos.
It is heavier than it looks. Good for staying put, less good if you carry a gig bag everywhere.
Anyone with a keyboard at home or in a classroom who wants the pedal to behave like a piano. If you are buying a keyboard for a kid, buy this with it.

verdict.buy: Your current pedal slides, feels like a toy, or you are setting up a keyboard for a beginner.
verdict.skip: You already have a weighted pedal with a rubber base. This will not be a big upgrade.

product: Weighted sustain pedal with polarity switch

title: The mic I record lessons with
short: Plug it in, hit record, sounds like a studio. No interface, no drivers, no fuss.

images.alt: USB microphone on a desk beside a laptop
Side view of the microphone on its stand

quickTake: One cable. Works on Mac, Windows, and iPad with a basic adapter.
The mute button on the mic is the feature I use most on Zoom.
Picks up a piano and a voice in the same take without clipping.

p: I record short lessons and webinars from my dining room. Laptop mics make a piano sound like a tin can. I did not want to learn an audio interface just to sound normal.
Set-up took two minutes. I have recorded a few hundred videos on it since. Nobody has ever asked what I use, which is the compliment you want from a microphone.

body.h: What to know before you buy
p: Put it on a boom arm or a towel if your desk is bouncy. It will pick up you typing.
Sit about a hand's width away. Any closer and plosives show up.
Teachers recording lessons, anyone on Zoom all day, and musicians who want a clean take without a studio. If you are already running an interface and XLR mics, you do not need this.

verdict.buy: You record on a laptop and want to sound clear without learning audio gear.
verdict.skip: You already own an interface and condenser mic. Keep what you have.

product: USB condenser microphone with mute button
